column3: Forgiveness, entry, gardens, rivers, and good dwellings present the requested abundance as a sustaining divine admission rather than proof of status.
The garden-and-river reward for truthful speech frames such abundance as God's recompense, though the formula is already well represented.
Pharaoh's claim over rivers exposes the contrary move of treating flowing provision as personal political possession.
Prepared, eternal gardens make the promise a divine provision for a defined response, but largely repeat the central formula.
The objection that a messenger eats and walks in markets supplies the immediate social expectation behind the luxury demand answered in 25:10.
Repentance leading to entry into rivered gardens makes the abundance part of restoration and protection, while repeating earlier evidence.
Rivered gardens set life-giving enclosure against the preceding fire and trench, giving the promise a sharp contrary setting.
The audible anger and exhalation of the distant fire supplies the immediate opposite destination to the better gardens of 25:10.
Its direct comparison of what is later as better than what is first supports the verse's corrective measure of betterment.
A demanded private garden with bursting rivers closely parallels the opponents' demand for visible, controlled wealth as proof.
The fire destination marks a broad contrast, but it adds little to the specific question of gardens, rivers, and palaces.
The claim that one may choose whatever one wishes challenges the assumption that demanded luxury can be treated as an entitlement.
Gardens and rivers appear among God's sustaining gifts, extending 25:10's abundance into communal provision and continuity.
The demand for a treasure or an edible private garden is the immediate contrast that 25:10 explicitly redirects to divine willing.
Its claim that one time is better than many supports comparative good only indirectly and does not address the requested material signs.
The same blessing formula and God's making of ordered heavenly signs reinforce divine creative capacity within the surah.
The accusation of fabrication continues the immediate opposition, but adds little to the particular abundance claim in 25:10.
Human willing is explicitly dependent on God's willing, directly clarifying the conditional authority in 25:10.
Entry into eternal rivered gardens with forgiveness presents the promise as salvation, though it is another close formula repetition.
Continued residence in the fire is a general negative counterpart with limited explanatory force for the focus verse.
Better than this followed by eternal rivered gardens closely matches 25:10's comparison and revalues desired possessions.
A stream placed beneath Mary offers a local image of provision, but not the garden-and-palace claim at issue.
The assertion that all earlier messengers ate and walked in markets directly normalizes the condition attacked in 25:7.
Flowing springs clarify that the water imagery denotes continuously available provision, although they duplicate the river motif.
Its rivered gardens and recurring provision reinforce permanence but add little after the stronger close parallels.
The opening blessing and universal warning establish the authority of the revealer before the opponents demand material credentials.
Garden residence without the focus verse's river, palace, or conditional grant gives only a loose reward parallel.
God's making of a settled earth, built sky, forms, and good provision supports the attribution of bounty to the divine maker.
The protected sign and common land connect only through a broad provision channel, not the requested abundance.
God's repentance toward whom He wills supports conditional mercy only indirectly.
The explicit "if God wills" qualifies human commitment and supports the focus verse's dependent conditionality.
Its direct question whether this is better or the eternal garden is the surah's clearest continuation of 25:10's comparison.
God creates and chooses while creatures have no independent choice, directly grounding who may grant the better alternative.
Night and day as signs do not materially clarify the requested gardens, rivers, or palaces.
God's stated ability to send a warner to every town reinforces that the actual form of prophetic provision follows divine choice.
Calling worship and God-consciousness better than alternatives gives a broad evaluative parallel without explaining the imagery.
Individual willing to remember is too general to illuminate the divine willing and promised abundance of 25:10.
The destruction of the designated camel is only a remote channel contrast to entrusted provision.
The rejected reading does not provide usable support for the focus verse.
God's making some barren shows divine discretion, but offers no close connection to the promised gardens or palaces.
The same-surah reply locates revelation in the one who knows secrets and forgives, countering the opponents' dismissive demands.
God's willing formation of a person supports the distinction between the creating giver and those who demand a sign of wealth.
The hope that God may replace a lost garden with something better gives a direct, though different, pattern of divinely given betterment.
The promised garden's rivers, lasting fruit, and shade specify the durable, self-renewing quality of the better gift.
Calling faithful workers the best of creation ties betterness to response and action rather than inherited display.
God's power to replace people with better ones supports the claim that betterment is under divine power and discretion.
Exclusive dominion, creation, and measure establish the authority that makes gardens and palaces a gift rather than a demanded proof.
It warns that people can mistake an urgently sought outcome for good, sharpening the critique of impatient material demands.
Faith itself occurs only by God's permission, supplying a broader parallel for the focus verse's dependence on divine willing.
The listed virtues connect to reward generally, but do not add a clear account of the requested abundance.
Wind running by God's command illustrates governed movement, but is distant from the garden-river and palace setting.
Enclosed companions in tents add a loose dwelling image without clarifying the focus verse's claim.
The ruined town in the same surah is a general warning, not a direct explanation of the better gardens and palaces.
Ships moving on the sea share an image of movement but do not clarify the promised flowing provision.
The choice to seek uprightness gives human willing a direction, which the surrounding passage then places under divine willing.
The defeated party gaining no good is a distant contrast to betterness and does not explain the focus imagery.
The movement and concealment reading is too remote from the verse's grant of gardens and palaces.
Palaces and carved homes received in the land show built grandeur as a bestowed condition, not an autonomous claim.
The charge that the revelation is copied continues the opponents' rhetoric but adds no specific connection to 25:10's answer.
Rain, fruits, ships, and rivers are explicitly subjected by God, grounding flowing provision in divine agency.
The possibility of much good beyond present dislike supports the corrective sense of "better," though in a different social setting.
God admits faithful actors into rivered gardens and does what He wills, closely combining reward imagery with divine discretion.
Gardens of bliss repeat the reward setting without adding the rivers, comparison, or challenge context.
A promised safe entry explicitly conditioned by God's willing supplies a close pattern of assured yet dependent fulfillment.
The garden companions have a better resting place, directly extending the surah's measure of what counts as better.
God as creator and guardian of everything supports the comprehensive authority presupposed by the offer of greater provision.
Sorting the foul from the good and gathering the foul for hell does not clarify the focus verse's promised abundance.
The fire's exhalation is a distant opposite image with little added value beyond 25:12.
Rivered gardens contrast with transient animal-like enjoyment and fire, but repeat the already established reward formula.
God as best at settling one gives a loose dwelling parallel, without the focus verse's comparison or material signs.
The denial that other gods control benefit, harm, life, or resurrection directly establishes why only God can grant the requested good.
Gardens and springs offer another reward image but add little after the many fuller rivered-garden passages.
Lengthy daytime activity does not clarify the focus verse.
Paired gardens and good provision portray abundance as a sign requiring gratitude, usefully contrasting acquisitive proof demands.
Gardens and a river join God-consciousness to a protected, supplied setting, though the imagery is now redundant.
The blessing formula, creation, and command reinforce that all ordered provision belongs to the Lord of the worlds.
Night, sleep, and day as divine arrangements are same-surah provision signs but only indirectly related to 25:10.
Finding greater good and reward with God supports deferred value, but not the verse's specific material imagery.
Wisdom as abundant good is a broad alternative account of good, with little link to the immediate controversy.
The making of houses for Moses' people is a distant dwelling parallel without a clear relation to the focus claim.
Human willing occurs only when God wills, directly reiterating the focus verse's governing condition.
Greeting the companions of the right adds no meaningful clarification of 25:10.
The scattering of deeds in the same surah is a general judgment contrast, not an explanation of divine abundance.
Human haste in calling evil as good supports misjudged desire only indirectly.
Divine enrichment and goodness appear in a different legal setting and add little to the requested sign debate.
The withdrawal of shade does not clarify the gardens, rivers, palaces, or divine comparison.
Receiving something better than one's good deed and safety from terror supports surplus divine recompense.
God could have enabled fighting but did not; this illustrates power and willing only at a very general level.
Regret over a companion does not add to the focus verse.
Guidance given or withheld by God gives a general discretion parallel but no close connection to the promised provision.
Human creation from a clinging substance does not clarify 25:10.
Calling recourse to God and the Messenger better concerns adjudication, not the focus verse's material comparison.
The prophet's refusal of wages does not clarify the focus verse.
God singles out whom He wills for mercy, a broad but limited parallel to the distribution of divine good.
No one can prevent God's intended act, and all dominion belongs to Him, directly reinforcing the conditional grant's authority.
Gardens and bliss provide only a terse, redundant reward parallel.
The insistence that all command belongs to God challenges claims of independent control, though it is far from the garden imagery.
Pharaoh's abandoned gardens and springs show that apparent possession is not secure authority, sharpening 25:10's gift-versus-ownership contrast.
Reviving a ruined town demonstrates divine power, but offers only a distant basis for the promise of better provision.
A garden given for patience repeats the reward setting without adding the comparison, rivers, or palaces.
The instruction to consider the opponents' examples identifies their demands as disorienting speech, directly framing the correction delivered in 25:10.
Their denial of the Hour exposes the eschatological horizon absent from their demand for immediately visible wealth.
Confinement in a narrow, chained place supplies a stark spatial opposite to the expansive gardens and palaces of 25:10.
The command to call for many destructions continues the fire contrast but adds less than the adjacent spatial image.
The eternal garden contains whatever its people wish and is God's binding promise, directly distinguishing fulfilled divine promise from the opponents' demanded display.
The demand to see angels or the Lord repeats the opponents' insistence that revelation meet their chosen evidentiary terms.
The demand for a spring from the earth closely parallels the demand for a garden with rivers as a public proof of prophethood.
A house of gold is an especially close counterpart to the palaces of 25:10 and exposes wealth as a demanded credential.
Desired worldly wealth, children, livestock, and cultivated land provide the material horizon against which 3:15 and 25:10 redefine what is better.
Gardens beneath which rivers flow, with adornment and resting places, develop the promise as an inhabited and honored setting.
The garden parable joins possession to "what God wills," resisting the owner's treatment of abundance as self-secured.
The possibility that God may give something better than a garden directly links divine discretion, garden wealth, and comparative good.
The warning not to extend one's eyes toward worldly splendor corrects the same visual economy of demanding wealth as validation.
The contrast between the harvest of the hereafter and the harvest of this world gives a broad frame for why immediate gain is not the final measure of good.
Worldly adornment and multiplication are declared transient, sharpening the distinction between displayed wealth and the enduring promised outcome.
